what: Axsome Therapeutics develops and sells medicines for disorders of the central nervous system. Its approved products include Auvelity for major depressive disorder, Sunosi for excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy and sleep apnoea, and Symbravo for migraine.
customers: Psychiatrists, neurologists and primary care doctors in the United States, with the cost borne by commercial insurers and government programmes.
money: Oral medicine for major depressive disorder with a different mechanism from standard antidepressants.
Wakefulness medicine for narcolepsy and obstructive sleep apnoea.
moat: The products are protected by patents and by the clinical data behind them, and Axsome built its own US sales force aimed at psychiatry, which is an asset in itself: reaching prescribers in this field takes years and money.
risks: The company is still loss-making: about $157.3M of net loss and roughly negative $82.6M of free cash flow in the trailing period.
Growth requires heavy spending on sales force and promotion, which is why revenue growth has not yet produced profit.
Depression is a crowded market full of cheap generics, so insurers push back hard on a branded, higher-priced option.
Cash of $322.9M against $211.4M of debt is not a large cushion for a company still burning cash.
Twenty-one analysts average a $264.62 target against a $135.68 price, a very wide gap that reflects binary outcomes rather than precision.
opportunities: Revenue has grown very fast, from $270.6M in 2023 to $638.5M in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $865.3M.
Several additional indications and pipeline programmes could expand the use of existing molecules without new discovery risk.
Operating leverage is high: once the sales force is built, additional prescriptions cost little to serve, so profitability could arrive quickly.
A commercial psychiatry platform with multiple products is an attractive asset to larger pharmaceutical companies.
watch: The point at which revenue growth outruns promotional spending. Axsome has proved it can sell; the open question is whether it can do so profitably, and the operating loss trend answers it.
